cues.text: Welcome to Organic Principles.
This is a recorded Chemistry class with an AI generated Marin voice.
Keep paper beside you: we will read structures, follow electrons, and check
our answers.
Start with carbon's bonds.
A single carbon to carbon bond is a sigma bond.
A double bond has one sigma and one pi bond.
A triple bond has one sigma and two pi bonds.
In ethene, the four carbon to hydrogen bonds contribute four sigma bonds, and
the double bond contributes one more sigma and one pi.
The total is five sigma and one pi.
Pause and count before continuing.
Now connect structure to shape.
A typical carbon with four single bonds is approximately tetrahedral and
described as s p three.
A double bonded carbon is usually approximately trigonal planar, s p two.
A carbon in a triple bond is approximately linear, s p.
Functional groups guide naming and reactivity.
An alcohol has an O H group attached to a saturated carbon.
An aldehyde has a terminal carbonyl carbon bonded to hydrogen.
Sharing a molecular formula does not guarantee the same functional group.
Let's name the branched alcohol on the board.
The parent containing the alcohol carbon has four carbons.
Number from the end that gives the O H group position two.
The methyl branch is then at position three.
The name is three methyl butan two ol.
Numbering the branch first would give the alcohol the wrong priority.
Count five carbons in total, because the branch contributes one.
There are twelve hydrogens, including the hydrogen on oxygen, so the molecular
formula is C five H twelve O.
A name should let you reconstruct the same connectivity, not merely sound
familiar.
Now ask whether two drawings represent different molecules or different ways
to
describe one molecule.
Ethanol and methoxymethane both have formula C two H six O.
Ethanol has an alcohol group.
Methoxymethane, also called dimethyl ether, has an oxygen between two methyl
groups.
Their connectivity differs, so they are functional group structural isomers.
Geometrical isomers are different spatial arrangements with the same
connectivity.
For an ordinary alkene to show this type of isomerism, each double bonded
carbon must have two different substituents.
Consider chloroethene on the board.
One double bonded carbon carries two identical hydrogens.
That fails the condition, so there is no cis trans pair.
In but two ene, each double bonded carbon carries hydrogen and methyl.
The methyl groups can be on the same side or opposite sides, giving cis and
trans.
Rotating your sheet of paper does not create a different isomer.
A tetrahedral carbon with four different groups can be a stereogenic centre,
but molecular symmetry still matters when assessing optical activity.
We will leave detailed stereochemical drawings for further practice.
Resonance is a different idea.
Its contributors keep nuclei and connectivity fixed.
Only electron placement changes.
Acetate has two equivalent oxygen atoms sharing the negative charge; the
actual
ion is a resonance hybrid.
It does not repeatedly turn from one contributor molecule into another.
If a proposed drawing moves a hydrogen from one carbon to another, it is not a
resonance contributor of that unchanged structure.
Before choosing an answer, ask three questions.
Is the molecular formula the same?
Is connectivity the same?
Did I move nuclei or only electrons?
Those checks separate several concepts that are often confused.
Electron arrows begin where electrons are.
In homolytic bond breaking, one electron goes to each fragment and radicals
result.
A fishhook arrow represents one electron.
In heterolytic breaking, both bonding electrons go to one fragment.
A full headed curved arrow represents a pair.
A nucleophile donates an electron pair to form a bond, and an electrophile
accepts that pair.
Charge is a useful clue but not a definition.
Ammonia is neutral and can donate its nitrogen lone pair.
Boron trifluoride is neutral overall but its electron deficient boron can
accept a pair.
Now follow hydroxide reacting with methyl bromide in a substitution.
The carbon to bromine bond is polarized, making carbon the accepting site.
Draw an arrow from an oxygen lone pair on hydroxide to that carbon.
At the same time, draw an arrow from the carbon to bromine bond to bromine.
One pair makes the new carbon to oxygen bond; another pair goes with the
leaving bromide.
The products are methanol and bromide.
For this concerted methyl substitution, do not invent a free methyl
carbocation
between those events.
Let's audit the equation.
The reactants contain one carbon, four hydrogens, one oxygen and one bromine.
Methanol and bromide contain exactly the same inventory.
Total charge is negative one on each side.
If your proposed products lose that charge, revisit the arrows.
Substitution replaces a group.
Addition introduces groups across a multiple bond; hydrogenation of ethene
gives ethane.
Elimination removes groups to form a multiple bond.
Rearrangement changes the arrangement of the skeleton or groups.
These labels describe the net change.
The substrate, solvent and reaction conditions still decide which pathway is
favoured.
Always read those conditions before applying a reaction pattern.
Stability rules are useful only when their assumptions fit.
The inductive effect describes polarization transmitted through sigma bonds
and
generally weakens with distance.
Resonance needs a connected set of suitable orbitals.
Hyperconjugation involves interaction of an adjacent sigma bond with a
suitable
empty or partly occupied orbital, or a pi system.
For simple comparable alkyl carbocations, donation and hyperconjugation often
favour tertiary over secondary over primary.
That is not permission to rank every carbocation by counting alkyl groups
alone.
An allylic or benzylic position can gain resonance stabilization.
Compare the two cations on the board.
In the three carbon allylic cation, the positive carbon sits directly beside
the double bond and has an empty p orbital.
Move the pi pair toward the cationic carbon.
The new contributor has the double bond at the other end and the positive
charge on the opposite terminal carbon.
The three carbon positions and their attached hydrogens stay fixed.
The total charge remains positive one.
This is direct allylic resonance.
Now add a saturated carbon between the double bond and the cationic carbon.
That intervening carbon interrupts the same uninterrupted p orbital system.
A double bond somewhere in the molecule is not enough.
This comparison tests direct conjugation; it does not calculate every
contribution to either ion's stability.
In elementary descriptions, the electromeric effect refers to complete
displacement of a pi pair under attack by a reagent.
Treat that as electron movement during a reaction, not as another name for a
permanent resonance hybrid.
When a question gives a stability comparison, locate the charge, look for
adjacent orbitals, then examine induction and hyperconjugation under the
stated
conditions.
Do that before reaching for a memorized ranking.
Our final example connects electron distribution to acidity.
Removing a proton gives a conjugate base.
Stabilizing that base can help explain why an acid donates a proton more
readily, when other factors are comparable.
Acetate delocalizes charge over two oxygens; an ordinary alkoxide lacks that
same arrangement.
But compare acids in the same solvent and at the same temperature.
Solvation and other effects matter, so a single structural slogan cannot
decide
every comparison.
Quantitatively, p K a is the negative base ten logarithm of K a.
Lower p K a means a larger acid dissociation constant and a stronger acid.
Suppose acid A has p K a three, while acid B has p K a five under the same
conditions.
Pause and calculate the ratio of their constants.
K a for A is ten to the minus three, and for B it is ten to the minus five.
Dividing gives ten squared, or one hundred.
A has the larger K a and is the stronger acid.
Its conjugate base is weaker than B's conjugate base in that same solvent.
We did not calculate a hydrogen ion concentration.
A ratio of equilibrium constants does not by itself establish a p H
difference;
concentration and the equilibrium problem still matter.
Finish by returning to our five checks.
Read the functional groups and count bonds.
Give naming priorities the correct order.
Distinguish structural isomers, spatial arrangements and resonance
contributors.
Start electron arrows at electron pairs and conserve atoms and charge.
Check that a proposed stabilization mechanism is actually available.
Use the twelve original practice questions below, and open the written
companion for all seven worked examples.
This recorded foundation supports Unit fourteen; it is not exhaustive organic
chemistry coverage and these questions are not official past papers.
When several functional groups occur in one molecule, identify the principal
group before numbering the parent.
For hydroxy carboxylic acids in these examples, the carboxylic acid supplies
the suffix and the alcohol is described by a hydroxy prefix.
In H O C H two, C H two, C O O H, the carboxyl carbon is
carbon one.
The parent contains three carbons, and the hydroxy group is on carbon three,
giving three hydroxypropanoic acid.
In C H three, C H with O H, C O O H, the hydroxy group is instead on carbon
two, giving two hydroxypropanoic acid.
These compounds have the same molecular formula but different connectivity.
Do not renumber from the alcohol end to give the prefix a lower number at the
expense of the principal acid group.
For the separate ketone C H three, C O, C H two, C H three, numbering gives
butan two one.
Draw the connectivity from a proposed name as a reverse check.
This short selection does not establish a complete priority hierarchy for
every
multifunctional molecule.
A degree of unsaturation counts rings and pi bond equivalents in ordinary
closed shell organic formulas with the usual valences.
Start with twice the carbon count plus two, add nitrogen, then subtract
hydrogen and the monovalent halogen count.
Divide by two.
Oxygen does not appear in this elementary expression.
For C four H eight O, the result is one.
The formula could describe an alkene, a carbonyl compound or a ring containing
compound; the index alone does not identify the functional group.
For C three H five chlorine, count chlorine like one hydrogen.
Eight minus five minus one, divided by two, again gives one.
A triple bond contributes two units, while one ring or one double bond
contributes one.
Benzene, C six H six, gives four: one ring and three double bond equivalents.
The index is a consistency check rather than a unique structure generator.
Unusual valence states, ions or radicals need additional care before applying
this simple formula.
A negative or unexpected fractional result should prompt a check of the
molecular formula and model assumptions.
Geometrical isomerism requires two different substituents on each carbon of an
ordinary alkene double bond.
The E and Z system compares the higher priority substituent on each end.
In the simple example drawn here, the left carbon bears bromine and hydrogen,
while the right bears chlorine and a methyl group.
Bromine outranks hydrogen because its directly attached atom has the higher
atomic number.
Chlorine outranks the methyl carbon for the same reason.
When bromine and chlorine lie on the same side of the double bond, the
arrangement is Z.
When those higher priority groups lie on opposite sides, it is E.
Do not compare the sizes of the printed group names or simply select the two
heaviest complete groups.
If directly attached atoms tie, the sequence rules require further comparisons
beyond this elementary example.
An alkene with two hydrogens on one end fails the starting condition, so an E
or Z label cannot be assigned there.
Cis and trans refer to specified relative groups and are not automatically
interchangeable with E and Z in every substituted alkene.
A tetrahedral carbon attached to four different groups is a common source of
molecular chirality.
Carbon two in butan two ol carries hydrogen, hydroxyl, methyl and ethyl
groups.
All four differ, so the molecule has a pair of nonsuperimposable mirror image
configurations.
By comparison, isopropyl alcohol has two identical methyl groups at its
alcohol
carbon and does not have that stereogenic centre.
The drawing uses a Fischer projection convention: horizontal attachments point
toward the viewer and vertical attachments point away.
Reflecting the left and right groups produces the opposite configuration in
this one centre example.
Turning a complete spatial molecule does not change its configuration.
An individual enantiomer can rotate plane polarized light, while an equal
mixture of the two gives cancelling rotations under the same conditions.
R and S descriptors specify configuration and do not automatically predict
positive or negative optical rotation.
With several stereogenic centres, two to the power of the centre count is a
maximum count under simple assumptions; molecular symmetry can reduce the
number.
Never decide overall chirality from carbon counting alone.
Formal charge checks whether an electron drawing is consistent with its stated
species.
Assign each atom its nonbonding electrons and half of the electrons in its
bonds, then compare with the neutral atom's valence count.
In ammonia, nitrogen has five valence electrons, one lone pair containing two
electrons, and three single bonds.
Its formal charge is five minus two minus three, or zero.
In ammonium, nitrogen has four single bonds and no lone pair, giving five
minus
zero minus four, or plus one.
In hydroxide, oxygen has six valence electrons, six nonbonding electrons and
one single bond, giving minus one.
Sum all atomic formal charges to obtain the species charge.
A full curved arrow represents movement of an electron pair and begins at a
pair or bond; a single headed fishhook represents one electron.
Formal charge is bookkeeping, rather than a direct measurement of partial
charge.
Resonance contributors preserve atomic positions and overall charge while
redistributing electrons.
Moving an attached hydrogen to another atom changes connectivity and is not
merely a resonance arrow.
Acidity comparisons should begin with the conjugate base and the conditions of
comparison.
In a matched carboxylic acid series, a nearby chlorine substituent withdraws
electron density through sigma bonds and can stabilize the conjugate base.
Chloroacetic acid is therefore stronger than acetic acid in the usual aqueous
comparison.
Moving that substituent farther from the acid group generally weakens the
inductive effect.
Resonance requires a suitable connected orbital system and is not the same as
this through bond polarization.
Acetate delocalizes negative charge between its two oxygens, whereas an
ordinary alkoxide lacks the same carboxylate arrangement.
Hybridization supplies another controlled comparison: a terminal alkyne is
more
acidic than corresponding simple alkene or alkane carbon hydrogen sites,
because its conjugate base places the lone pair in an orbital with greater s
character.
These examples do not imply one effect dominates every molecule.
Solvation, substituent position, competing resonance and the actual proton
removed can change a ranking.
State the structures and medium instead of treating the words electron
withdrawing as a complete explanation.
A proton transfer equilibrium connects two acid dissociation constants
measured
in the same solvent at the same temperature.
Write H A plus base B forming A minus plus the conjugate acid H B plus.
The equilibrium constant equals the acid constant of H A divided by the acid
constant of H B plus.
In terms of p K a, this is ten raised to the p K a of H B plus minus the p K a
of H A.
With illustrative values five and nine respectively, the exponent is nine
minus
five, or four, and the constant is ten thousand.
Products are favoured in that defined equilibrium.
Reversing the equation gives the reciprocal constant, one ten thousandth.
This calculation does not establish a p H or percentage conversion without
starting concentrations and the appropriate mass and charge balances.
Do not mix aqueous values with values measured in a different solvent as if
the
numbers shared one scale.
The useful direction rule is that proton transfer tends to favour the weaker
acid and weaker base pair, while the numerical equilibrium expression makes
that comparison precise.
Rotation about a single bond changes conformation without changing the atom
connectivity.
View ethane along its carbon carbon bond using a Newman projection.
When the front and rear carbon hydrogen bonds line up in the view, the
arrangement is eclipsed.
A sixty degree rotation produces a staggered arrangement, where the rear bonds
lie between the front bonds.
In the usual ethane torsional picture, staggered arrangements are energy
minima
and eclipsed arrangements are maxima.
Equivalent patterns repeat every one hundred twenty degrees because each
carbon
carries three identical hydrogens.
These conformers normally interconvert rapidly at ordinary temperatures and
are
not a new set of constitutional isomers.
The torsional energy difference is also not the energy required to break the
carbon carbon sigma bond.
Larger molecules introduce additional steric interactions, so one ethane
picture does not rank every substituted conformation.
Changing an alkene from E to Z instead changes its double bond configuration
and is not achieved by unrestricted ordinary single bond rotation about that
double bond.
Identify which bond rotates and whether connectivity or configuration changes
before naming the relationship.
An R or S label describes a spatial arrangement, not the sign of optical
rotation.
Consider a tetrahedral carbon attached to bromine, chlorine, fluorine and
hydrogen.
Their directly attached atomic numbers give priorities bromine first, chlorine
second, fluorine third and hydrogen fourth.
In the stated viewing diagram, hydrogen points directly away from the viewer.
Bromine is at the top, chlorine at the lower right and fluorine at the lower
left.
Following priorities one, two and three is clockwise, so this arrangement is
R.
Interchanging the chlorine and fluorine positions gives S.
If the lowest priority group points toward the viewer instead, the apparent
clockwise or anticlockwise result must be reversed.
Rotating a molecule in space does not interchange its configuration, while
exchanging one pair of groups reverses a single tetrahedral centre.
This example avoids priority ties; comparing carbon chains or multiple bonds
requires additional sequence rules.
Do not infer a positive optical rotation from R or a negative rotation from S:
that relationship requires experimental information.
A mixture containing two enantiomers can have unequal amounts without being a
pure enantiomer.
Suppose a sample contains seventy percent R and thirty percent S by amount,
with no other components.
Enantiomeric excess is the absolute difference, forty percent in favour of R.
It is not seventy percent.
Conversely, forty percent excess of one enantiomer means seventy percent major
and thirty percent minor, because their fractions sum to one as well as
differing by zero point four zero.
In a supplied ideal linear optical rotation model, suppose pure R has specific
rotation plus fifty under fixed solvent, temperature and wavelength
conditions.
Pure S then has minus fifty under the same conditions, and the mixture has
plus
twenty.
This inference assumes only that enantiomeric pair contributes and the stated
additive model applies.
The sign assigned to R is supplied experimental information, not a consequence
of the R label.
Zero net rotation can result from a racemic mixture, but it does not prove
every molecule is achiral.
Other components or changing measurement conditions can invalidate a simple
excess calculation.
The products of bond cleavage depend on where the two bonding electrons go.
In homolytic cleavage of a neutral single bond, one electron goes to each
fragment.
The elementary products are two radicals, represented with dots for unpaired
electrons, and electron movement uses single headed fishhook arrows.
In heterolytic cleavage, both bonding electrons go to one fragment.
For the stated neutral A B bond with both electrons assigned to B, the
elementary products are A plus and B minus, shown with a full headed curved
arrow from the bond toward B.
Overall charge is conserved in both descriptions.
The labels do not imply that any chosen bond will cleave spontaneously, or
that
isolated ions remain stable in every solvent.
Bond energy, light, temperature, solvent and the surrounding mechanism
determine which pathway is relevant.
Radicals are not automatically positively charged, and a negative ion can have
paired electrons.
Start each electron arrow at an existing electron source and keep electron
count separate from formal charge when checking a proposed elementary step.
Keto enol tautomerism and resonance are different structural relationships.
Acetone has three carbon atoms, six hydrogens and one oxygen.
A corresponding enol has a carbon carbon double bond, an oxygen hydrogen bond
and the same overall molecular formula.
In this interconversion, a hydrogen changes its attachment and the positions
of
the double bonds change.
The two neutral structures are constitutional isomers that can be in chemical
equilibrium, not alternative resonance drawings of one fixed atomic
arrangement.
By contrast, resonance contributors of an enolate keep every atom in place and
differ in electron placement and formal charges.
Acetone has six alpha hydrogens on two symmetry equivalent methyl groups;
these
give one distinct constitutional monoenol connectivity.
This statement does not count different conformations.
The simple enolization route needs an alpha hydrogen on a carbon adjacent to
the carbonyl.
The equilibrium proportion is not fixed at fifty percent and depends on the
actual compound and conditions.
Recognize whether a drawing changes an atom attachment before choosing an
equilibrium arrow or a resonance arrow.
Priority rules compare the atoms directly attached to a stereogenic centre
before considering the rest of each group.
Oxygen outranks carbon because its atomic number is larger, even if the carbon
substituent has a much greater total mass.
If the directly attached atoms tie, compare the attached atom lists in
descending atomic number order until the first difference.
An ethyl group starts with a carbon attached onward to carbon, hydrogen and
hydrogen.
A methyl carbon instead has hydrogen, hydrogen and hydrogen, so ethyl outranks
methyl.
A hydroxymethyl carbon has oxygen, hydrogen and hydrogen and outranks ethyl at
that first comparison.
For multiple bonds, use the standard duplicate atom convention: an aldehyde
carbon attached to oxygen by a double bond is compared using oxygen, oxygen
and
hydrogen.
It therefore outranks hydroxymethyl in this comparison.
Isotopes of the same element are ranked by mass number, so deuterium outranks
ordinary hydrogen.
Do not sum the atomic numbers in a whole substituent or rank groups by
molecular mass.
Establish the ordered groups first, then apply the viewing direction needed
for
an R or S assignment.
The familiar two to the power n count is a maximum for n independent
tetrahedral stereocentres, not a guaranteed count for every molecule.
Consider two three dibromobutane, whose two stereogenic carbons lie between
identical methyl ends.
The formal assignments R R and S S give a pair of nonsuperimposable mirror
images.
The mixed assignments R S and S R instead describe the same meso stereoisomer
after the molecular symmetry is recognized.
This form is achiral overall despite containing two stereogenic centres.
There are therefore three configurational stereoisomers rather than four: one
enantiomeric pair and one meso form.
A meso sample is not a fifty fifty mixture of two enantiomers.
Its lack of optical activity follows from the achiral molecular structure,
while a racemic mixture has cancellation between equal amounts of opposite
enantiomers under ordinary matched conditions.
Nor does every molecule with one R and one S centre have to be meso.
The substituent pattern and a valid symmetry or superposition argument must
support that conclusion.
Check actual connectivity and identical ends before reducing the maximum
stereoisomer count.
Rotation about the central carbon carbon single bond of butane changes
conformation without changing connectivity or configurational stereocentres.
In a Newman projection viewed along carbon two to carbon three, each visible
carbon carries a methyl group and two hydrogens.
In the anti staggered arrangement, the methyl groups are separated by a
dihedral angle of one hundred eighty degrees.
In either gauche staggered arrangement, their separation is sixty degrees in
one direction or the other.
Both are staggered, but they are not equal in energy: the anti form is lower
in
the usual introductory comparison because the methyl groups are farther apart.
The fully eclipsed arrangement with methyl groups aligned has a larger steric
and torsional penalty.
The two gauche positions do not mean two new constitutional compounds, and
rapid rotation means a sample need not remain frozen in its lowest energy
drawing.
At ordinary conditions more than one conformation can be populated.
Read the front carbon bonds from the central point and the rear carbon bonds
from the surrounding circle.
A flat sketch without that viewing convention can hide which groups actually
overlap.
A systematic isomer count needs a defined class and a rule for avoiding
duplicate drawings.
For ordinary neutral acyclic saturated compounds with formula four carbons,
ten
hydrogens and one oxygen, consider alcohols and ethers.
Alcohols can use the straight four carbon skeleton with hydroxyl at carbon one
or carbon two, giving butan one ol and butan two ol.
The branched skeleton gives two methylpropan one ol and two methylpropan two
ol.
These are four alcohol connectivities.
For ethers, split the four carbons between the two oxygen bonded groups as one
plus three or two plus two.
A methyl group can join either a straight propyl or an isopropyl group, giving
two ether connectivities.
Two ethyl groups give a third.
Reversing the left and right groups around oxygen does not make another
constitutional isomer.
Thus there are seven constitutional isomers in the stated class.
Butan two ol has a stereogenic carbon and two enantiomers, so counting
individual configurational forms instead gives eight total structures under
that different convention.
State whether stereoisomers are being distinguished before presenting a single
number.
An electron count is useful only after the structural conditions for cyclic
conjugation are checked.
In the simple Hückel treatment, an aromatic ring has suitable overlapping p
orbitals around a planar cycle and four n plus two pi electrons, with n a
nonnegative integer.
Benzene has six pi electrons.
The cyclopentadienyl anion also has six: two double bonds contribute four and
the appropriately oriented lone pair at the negatively charged carbon
contributes two.
The corresponding neutral cyclopentadiene has a saturated carbon interrupting
the continuous p orbital ring, so the same aromatic description does not
apply.
A planar fully conjugated closed shell four n electron model is antiaromatic,
but a molecule can avoid that geometry.
Cyclooctatetraene has eight pi electrons yet normally adopts a nonplanar tub
form and is classified as nonaromatic in this introductory comparison.
Do not label every eight electron ring antiaromatic without checking its shape
and orbital continuity.
A negative charge is not itself an aromaticity label, and aromatic does not
mean every bond is an isolated alternating single or double bond.
This chapter treats simple ring models; fused systems and advanced excited
state rules require additional analysis.
A carbocation rearrangement is electron pair movement, not a hydrogen nucleus
jumping independently of electrons.
Label a five carbon example as a four carbon chain C one through C four, with
a
methyl branch C five attached at C three.
Begin with the positive charge at C two and one hydrogen on C three.
The initial carbon two cation is secondary.
In the stated one two hydride shift, the C three hydrogen bond pair moves
toward the electron deficient C two site, making a new C two hydrogen bond.
Carbon two becomes a neutral methylene group, while carbon three becomes the
positive tertiary carbon.
The formula remains carbon five hydrogen eleven with overall charge plus one.
No carbon has left, no new hydrogen reagent was added, and the migrating
hydrogen does not appear as a free hydride ion in solution in this
description.
The curved arrow begins at the original C three hydrogen bond, not at the
positive charge.
Such a path can lead to a more stabilized cation when geometry and kinetics
permit, but a stability ranking alone does not prove every substrate
rearranges.
The supplied local step does not specify the final nucleophile capture product
or a complete reaction mechanism.
A Fischer projection encodes three dimensional bond directions, so
manipulating
its cross is not arbitrary artwork.
Horizontal bonds point toward the viewer and vertical bonds away.
Consider glyceraldehyde drawn with aldehyde at the top, hydroxymethyl below,
hydroxyl at the right and hydrogen at the left.
Priorities are hydroxyl first, aldehyde second, hydroxymethyl third and
hydrogen fourth.
The carbon substituents tie initially, but the aldehyde comparison list oxygen
oxygen hydrogen outranks oxygen hydrogen hydrogen.
Applying the toward viewer correction for the horizontal hydrogen gives R for
this drawing.
Rotating the whole Fischer drawing on the page by one hundred eighty degrees
preserves that configuration.
Rotating its labels by ninety degrees and interpreting the resulting cross
afresh with horizontal bonds toward and vertical bonds away instead represents
the opposite single centre configuration.
That is a changed projection interpretation, not a claim that physically
turning a molecule in space changes its handedness.
Interchanging one pair of substituents likewise inverts a single tetrahedral
centre, while two pair exchanges preserve it.
R and S still do not determine the measured sign of optical rotation.
Use these rules for the stated single centre rather than assuming every multi
centre manipulation has the same net effect.
Cis and trans describe chosen relative groups, whereas E and Z compare the
higher priority substituent at each alkene carbon.
Use two bromo but two ene, with a methyl and bromine on carbon two, and a
methyl and hydrogen on carbon three.
Each double bond carbon has two different substituents, so E and Z are
defined.
Bromine outranks the methyl carbon on the left, while the methyl carbon
outranks hydrogen on the right.
Now draw the two methyl groups on the same side of the double bond.
They are cis relative to one another, but the priority groups bromine and the
other methyl are on opposite sides, giving E.
Putting the methyl groups opposite makes that relative description trans,
while
the two higher priority groups are now together, giving Z.
Nothing about the double bond changed except the chosen geometrical
arrangement; the descriptor systems answer different comparisons.
This example does not make cis universally equal to E either.
For but two ene, methyl groups are the higher priority pair and cis
corresponds
to Z.
If one alkene carbon bears identical groups, the starting condition fails and
neither E nor Z can be assigned to that ordinary double bond.
